passage:
Sunaina, wait. Don't press send yet. Is that your school photo and our address you're pasting into that chatbot? Come, sit with your Farhan Mamu for one minute.

When I was fifteen, there was a public forum for cricket fans. I loved it. Someone asked where I lived so they could "send a signed poster." I posted my full address, my school name and a photo in my uniform. I thought it was just a chat.

Two weeks later, a man was waiting outside my school, calling my name. He knew my class. I ran back inside to the guard. Your Nani came to fetch me, white as paper. The police told us later my details had been copied to other sites.

Nothing terrible happened. But I never forgot the fear on her face.

A chatbot feels private. It isn't. What you type can be stored and seen. Ask it for help with your essay, fine. But your face, our address, your school? Treat it like a crowded street. Now, delete that, and let's write it without them.

qa.q: What did young Farhan post on the cricket forum?
qa.a: He posted his full address, his school name and a photo in his uniform.

qa.q: What was young Farhan feeling when the man called his name outside school?
qa.a: He felt frightened, which is why he ran back inside to the guard.

qa.q: What choice does Farhan Mamu want Sunaina to make, and why?
qa.a: He wants Sunaina to delete the photo, address and school details and ask for help without them, because a chatbot is not a private space.

qa.q: What was it like for Nani when she came to fetch Farhan?
qa.a: Nani was terrified, white as paper, realising strangers knew where her son studied.

grounding: It shows a teen about to paste a photo and home address into a chatbot, and an elder's story showing why such tools should be treated as public spaces for private identity information.

passage:
The scholarship form closed at midnight, and it was 11:35. Sarita's laptop battery was at nine per cent and the essay box still said "Tell us about yourself (300 words)."

"I'll just ask the chatbot to write it from my details," she muttered. She started pasting: her full name, her photo, her ID card number, her home address, her father's phone number, even the name of her school.

Her friend Vinita, on a video call, leaned closer. "Wait. Why does it need your ID number and address to write an essay?"

Sarita paused. "It… doesn't, I guess."

"Then don't give it. You don't know where that goes. It's like shouting your address on a railway platform."

The clock said 11:41. Sarita deleted everything except "Class 12 student who loves chemistry and teaches her younger cousins." She asked the chatbot for a structure, then wrote the essay herself, fast.

She submitted at 11:56, with two per cent battery. Her ID number stayed on the form, where it belonged.

qa.q: What time did the scholarship form close?
What was Sarita feeling as she rushed to finish?
qa.a: Sarita felt rushed and stressed, with the deadline close and the battery low.

qa.q: What did Sarita do after Vinita's warning, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Sarita deleted her private details and asked only for a structure, because a chatbot should be treated like a public space for identity information.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Sarita's rush?
qa.a: Vinita seems worried that the hurry made Sarita careless, which is why she stepped in with a simple question.

grounding: It shows a teen about to paste her photo, address and ID into a chatbot under time pressure, and choosing to treat it as a public space and keep private identity information out.
